INTRODUTION¶

As the NBA finals draw closer and closer, our group decided to choose a dataset that compares the National Basketball Association (NBA) player salaries. All four of us are very interested in sports and we definitely think this would be an interesting comparison to make because it’s a great opportunity to practice turning real raw data into insights. Salaries can provide an insight into teams' goals and values on the court. They can also provide information about a player's skill and value. There are many questions one can ask just from looking at salaries:

  • Does player performance justify the salary these players are getting?
  • How does the team’s overall spending affect their success?
  • How do salaries vary by position or experience?
  • What is the financial value of a player's statistical contribution?
  • Which player metrics matter most for salary?
  • Who are the best value players over the last 5 years?
  • What does this say about how NBA teams value different skill sets?

These are all questions that can be analyzed just from looking at player statistics and their salaries. Our group is most interested in how all this data that is gathered about these players can help predict the salary of a player and also which key statistics of a player (points, all-star status, etc.) are of most importance which in turn shows what teams value.

DATA CURATION¶

In this sction we will show and explain how we gathered, cleaned, and transformed raw data into structured dataframes, allowing us to analyze and draw conclusions about player statistics alongside player slaries.

We worked with two datasets that use real world datasets focused on NBA players.

NBA Salaries: Hoops Fortune (2020-2025)

This dataset, compiled and uploaded to Kaggle, contains detailed salary information for NBA players covering the seasons from 2020 to 2025. It provides annual salary figures and player names.

NBA Stats (1947-present)

These collection of datasets, also hosted on Kaggle, includes a comprehensive range of player statistics stretching from 1947 to the present. It features various performance metrics such as points per game, rebounds, assists, shooting percentages, and more.

Our team merged and titled many these two datasets to create unified tables linking player performance statistics with their corresponding salary data. These combined datasets serve as the foundation for our analyses and insights into how player performance correlates with financial compensation in the NBA.

We’ll begin by importing our datasets and preparing them for analysis. This included preprocing such as droping columns that are unused, merging dataframe together and organizing the into clean, structured formats.

Each method will help us answer important questions about player performance and salaries, and each conclusion will be supported by at least one visually compelling plot to bring our findings to life.

Method 2.A: One way ANOVA test¶

Question: Is mean salary significantly different depending on position?

Null Hypothesis: Mean salary is not statistically significant different depending on position.

Alternative Hypothesis: Mean salary is statistically significant different depending on position.

In [187]:

Method 2.B: T test¶

H0 (null hypothesis): There is no significant difference between the average salaries of 2022/2023 and 2023/2024

H1 (alternative hypothesis): There is a significant difference between the average salaries of 2022/2023 and 2023/2024.

In order to test this, a paired t-test is needed. We are only including players who have salary values for both seasons.

In [189]:
# clean up the salary columns
salaries_TTest.columns = ["player", "2022/2023", "2023/2024"]
salaries_TTest["2022/2023"] = salaries_TTest["2022/2023"].replace(r"[\$,]", "", regex=True).astype(float)
salaries_TTest["2023/2024"] = salaries_TTest["2023/2024"].replace(r"[\$,]", "", regex=True).astype(float)

# drop rows iwth missing or zero salaries for either year
paired_df = salaries_TTest[(salaries_TTest["2022/2023"] > 0) & (salaries_TTest["2023/2024"] > 0)].copy()

# perform paired t-test (ttest_rel performs a t-test on two related samples ttest_rel(a, b))

t_stat, p_val = ttest_rel(paired_df['2022/2023'], paired_df['2023/2024'])
print(f"Paired T-Test Results:")
print(f"T-statistic: {t_stat}")
print(f"P-value: {p_val}")

# Conclusion
alpha = 0.05
if p_val < alpha:
    print("Reject the null hypothesis: Salaries changed significantly.")
else:
    print("Fail to reject the null hypothesis: No significant salary change.")

Paired T-Test Results:
T-statistic: -6.835436760690918
P-value: 2.991643065086199e-11
Reject the null hypothesis: Salaries changed significantly.

Method 3: Linear Regression Model with Scatter plots AND Bar plots of coefficients¶

Coeffiecient Plot: Does Performance Predict Salary?

Coeffiecient plots can be used to visualize the weights that are assigned to a variable. In this case a positive coeffiecient show that an increase in that variable will increase salary, where a negative coeffiecient shows a decrease in salary as the variable increases. Neither positve or negative (zero coeffiecients) show there is no impact on the salary.

Regression Models:

  • Is Age Related to Salary?
  • Is Experience Related to Salary?
  • Is salary proportional to minutes played?

A regression model fits a “line” (or hyperplane) that best predicts a numeric outcome (like salary) from one or more variables. Positve slopes shows in this case salary increases as the variable increases, and negative slopes show that as a variable incrases salary decreases.

Starting with our coeffiecient plot, it answers the question: "Does Performance Predict Salary?"

We examine whether core performance metrics—like points, rebounds, assists—have a significant influence on player salaries. Using a linear regression model, we assess how much each statistic contributes to changes in pay. Scatter plots visualize relationships, while bar plots of regression coefficients show which performance stats carry the most weight financially.

In [192]:
# Does Performance Predict Salary?  
df_cleaned = gold_df[['ws', 'vorp', 'bpm', 'per', 'ts_percent', 'Salary']].dropna()

X = df_cleaned[['ws', 'vorp', 'bpm', 'per', 'ts_percent']].rename(columns={
    'ws': 'Win Shares',
    'vorp': 'Value Over Replacement Player',
    'bpm': 'Box Plus/Minus',
    'per': 'Player Efficiency Rating',
    'ts_percent': 'True Shooting Percentage'
})

y = df_cleaned['Salary']


model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
model.fit(X_scaled, y)
std_coefs = pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X.columns)

coefs_sorted = std_coefs.sort_values()

plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.hlines(y=coefs_sorted.index, xmin=0, xmax=coefs_sorted.values, color="skyblue")
plt.plot(coefs_sorted.values, coefs_sorted.index, "o")
plt.axvline(0, color="grey", linestyle="--")
plt.title("Effect Player Performance Has On Player Salary")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient Value (Effect on Salary)")
plt.ylabel("Performance Metric")
plt.show()

general_change = std_coefs.copy()

mean_salary = y.mean()
for metric in general_change.index:
    realistic_change = X[metric].std()  # Using 1 standard deviation change
    dollar_impact = general_change[metric] * realistic_change
    pct_impact = (dollar_impact / mean_salary) * 100
    print(f"{metric}: 1 SD change ({realistic_change:.1f}) → ${dollar_impact:,.0f} ({pct_impact:.1f}% of avg salary)")

change = general_change * X.std()
change = change.sort_values()

Win Shares: 1 SD change (2.4) → $2,103,947 (28.8% of avg salary)
Value Over Replacement Player: 1 SD change (1.1) → $6,077,465 (83.1% of avg salary)
Box Plus/Minus: 1 SD change (4.3) → $-3,239,977 (-44.3% of avg salary)
Player Efficiency Rating: 1 SD change (5.6) → $12,592,377 (172.1% of avg salary)
True Shooting Percentage: 1 SD change (0.1) → $-104,229 (-1.4% of avg salary)

Overall, performance metrics show a significant impact on salary, though not all in the same direction:

  • Player Efficiency Rating (PER) has the strongest positive effect, where a one standard deviation increase predicts an average salary increase of ~$12.6 million, equivalent to 172.1% of the average salary. This suggests teams heavily reward players with higher overall efficiency.

  • Value Over Replacement Player (VORP) and Win Shares also positively influence salary by ~$6.1 million (83.1%) and ~$2.1 million (28.8%), respectively, indicating that players contributing more wins or exceeding replacement-level performance are valued financially.

  • Interestingly, Box Plus/Minus shows a negative coefficient, predicting a ~$3.2 million (−44.3%) decrease for a one SD increase. This may reflect statistical noise, multicollinearity, or the possibility that extreme values in BPM might correlate with other factors like inconsistent roles.

  • True Shooting Percentage (TS%) has a minimal effect, with only about a $104K change (−1.4% of average salary) per SD shift, suggesting pure scoring efficiency alone may not strongly drive salaries without broader context.

Conclusion: Key performance metrics like PER and VORP strongly predict higher salaries, while some advanced stats like Box Plus/Minus show unexpected negative relationships, warranting further exploration.

Next, this regression models will answer the question: "Is Age Related to Salary?"

Younger players may earn less due to rookie contracts, while veteran players might command higher salaries—or decline due to age. Here, we model the relationship between age and salary to determine if there’s a clear trend, visualized with scatter plots and a regression line.

In [193]:
# Is Age Related to Salary?        
age_salary = gold_df.dropna(subset=["age", "Salary"])

plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))
sns.regplot(
    data=age_salary,
    x="age",
    y="Salary",
    scatter_kws={"alpha":0.5},
    line_kws={"color":"red"}
)
plt.title("Relationship between Age and Salary")
plt.xlabel("Age")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

There’s a slight positive relationship between age and salary. The regression line slopes upward, indicating older players tend to earn more, possibly reflecting accrued experience, veteran contracts, or established reputations.

However, the spread of data widens significantly for players above ~30 years old, suggesting high salary variance among veterans. Some older players still earn low salaries, perhaps due to declining performance, injuries, or minimum contracts.

Conclusion: Age modestly predicts higher salary, but variability increases as players age, showing that veteran status alone isn’t a guarantee of high pay.

This next regression model answers: "Is Experience Related to Salary?"

This analysis tests whether years of NBA experience correlate with higher salaries. Do veteran players consistently earn more, or is the relationship less predictable? A regression plot shows the strength and direction of the trend.

In [194]:
# Is Experience Related to Salary?  
exp_df = df_player_totals.merge(
    salary_long,
    on=["player", "season"],
    how="inner"
).dropna(subset=["experience", "Salary"])

plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))
sns.regplot(
    data=exp_df,
    x="experience",
    y="Salary",
    scatter_kws={"alpha":0.5},
    line_kws={"color":"green"}
)
plt.title("Relationship between Experience and Salary")
plt.xlabel("Years of Experience")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

Years of experience show a clearer positive relationship with salary than age. The regression trend suggests salaries generally rise as players accumulate seasons in the NBA.

Notably, salaries increase steeply in the first 5–10 years of experience—likely driven by players moving off rookie deals into more lucrative contracts. Beyond ~15 years, the slope flattens, reflecting that very experienced veterans may not always secure large contracts.

Conclusion: Experience strongly correlates with higher salaries, underscoring how players gain financial rewards as they build their careers and reputations.

These last regression model will answer both: "Is salary proportional to minutes played?" and "Is salary proportional to minutes per game?"

Playing time is often a proxy for value: coaches allocate more minutes to their best players. We analyze whether salary scales proportionally with minutes played per game, using scatter plots to check linearity and a regression model to quantify the relationship.

In [195]:
# Is salary proportional to minutes played?

sns.lmplot(data=gold_df, x='mp', y='Salary', height=5, aspect=1.5, line_kws={"color":"purple"})
plt.title("Is Salary Proportional to Minutes Played?")
plt.show()

# Merge per-game with salary
mp_df = df_player_per_game.merge(
    salary_long, on=['player', 'season'], how='inner'
)

sns.lmplot(data=mp_df, x='mp_per_game', y='Salary', height=5, aspect=1.5, line_kws={"color":"purple"})
plt.ylim(-0.05, None)   # Force y-axis lower bound to -0.05
plt.title("Is Salary Proportional to Minutes Per Game?")
plt.show()

Both plots show a positive relationship between playing time and salary:

Total minutes played and salary are clearly correlated—players logging more minutes earn higher salaries, reflecting their value and importance to their teams.

Minutes per game also correlate with higher pay, but the scatter shows greater variance. While stars playing 30+ minutes per game typically earn more, there are clusters of lower-paid players averaging high minutes, suggesting specific team situations or contract structures.

Conclusion: Playing time is a significant predictor of salary. Coaches allocate more minutes to their most trusted players, and the data confirms those players are financially rewarded.

PRIMARY ANALYSIS + VISUALIZATION¶

Can we predict NBA salaries from player stats, and learn which stats matter most?

Regression is definitely the most appropriate machine learning model for our goal. We are trying to predict what an NBA player should be paid and a player’s salary is a continuous numerical value. Regression tasks are usually designed for output variables that are quantitative like dollar amount. Additionally, we are not categorizing players into salary brackets, which would be more classification and we are not grouping them based on similarities, which would be clustering. Instead, we are estimating a salary amount based on their features.

We selected multiple linear regression, a supervised machine learning technique, as our primary analysis to predict NBA player salaries based on performance metrics. This method is ideal because:

  • Salary is a continuous numeric target variable.

  • We wanted interpretability to understand which player statistics have the most financial impact.

  • Linear regression allows us to quantify the effect of each metric on salary, answering our core question: Does player performance justify salary?

  • Our results indicate that metrics like PER and VORP significantly increase predicted salary, while others like BPM showed unexpected negative coefficients, suggesting complex dynamics in NBA contracts.

We can start by prepariing the Data Loaders, test_lader and train_loader. We will use test_train_split to split the data and then normalize it to make a zero mean and unit vairance. Taking the dataframe, 'df_cleaned' from method 3 above, we can implement an MLP to predict the salary of a given player.

In [196]:
# Using 'df_cleaned' from the coeff plot in method 3.
 
# normalize y to a better range of numbers so MSE is not off ( without it, the loss curve shows that the MLPmagnitudeis too high due to the large scale of salaries.)
new_y = df_cleaned['Salary'] / 1e6
# split data
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, new_y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# convert to float tensors
X_train_tensor = torch.FloatTensor(X_train_scaled)
y_train_tensor = torch.FloatTensor(y_train.values).view(-1, 1)

X_test_tensor = torch.FloatTensor(X_test_scaled)
y_test_tensor = torch.FloatTensor(y_test.values).view(-1, 1)

# Create datasets
train_dataset = TensorDataset(X_train_tensor, y_train_tensor)
test_dataset = TensorDataset(X_test_tensor, y_test_tensor)

batch_size = 32

# Create DataLoaders
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)

# Extra info if needed:
batch_size = train_loader.batch_size
num_train_data = len(train_loader) * batch_size
num_test_data = len(test_loader) * batch_size
feat_dim = train_loader.dataset[0][0].shape[0]

Next we will implement the MLP with layers and relu activation

In [197]:
class MLPModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        super(MLPModel, self).__init__()
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(input_dim, 64)
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(64, 32)
        self.output = nn.Linear(32, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.relu(self.layer1(x))
        x = torch.relu(self.layer2(x))
        x = self.output(x)
        return x

model = MLPModel(input_dim=feat_dim)

Next we create a loss function and optimizer, then train the model using epochs

In [198]:
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)

epochs = 100

batch_losses = []
epoch_losses = []

train_r2_scores = []
validate_r2_scores = []

for epoch in range(epochs):
    running_loss = 0.0
    for data, targets in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(data)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        batch_losses.append(loss.item())
        running_loss += loss.item()
    
    avg_loss = running_loss / len(train_loader)
    epoch_losses.append(avg_loss)

    # calculate R2 each epoch
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        train_preds = model(X_train_tensor)
        r2_train = r2_score(y_train_tensor.numpy(), train_preds.numpy())

        test_preds = model(X_test_tensor)
        r2_val = r2_score(y_test_tensor.numpy(), test_preds.numpy())

        train_r2_scores.append(r2_train)
        validate_r2_scores.append(r2_val)
    model.train()

    print(f"Epoch [{epoch+1}/{epochs}] - Avg Loss: {avg_loss:.4f} - "
          f"Train R2: {r2_train:.4f} - Val R2: {r2_val:.4f}")

INSIGHT & CONCLUSION¶

Looking at the loss plot, we can see that because the graph is decreasing over time, the model is learning how to predict NBA salaries. The MLP was trained to predict NBA salaries based on player statistics, with training loss measured via Mean Squared Error (MSE) (per millions).

As the model trains, it’s getting better at learning how NBA player stats relate to salaries. Early on, its predictions were way off. But the average prediction error has dropped significantly over time, suggesting the MLP is indeed capturing meaningful patterns between player performance and salary.

Unlike linear regression, the MLP does not produce direct coefficients explaining how much each stat contributes to salary. However, it offers a flexible alternative for pure predictive accuracy.

Taking in account of our regression models and and this MLP we can say that an NBA players stats do leave an impact on their pay in various ways, both positive and negative, given by the results of or regression models. The multiple linear regression shows that player stats do have a learnable relationship to salary and that it is possible for the model to predict a players salary given enough time.

The R2 train and validation curves provide some insight as well. Like the loss curve, it starts out poor and over time imporved as training progressed confiming the MLP was learning meaningful patterns from the data. The close alignment between training and validation R2 suggests the MLP generalizes well and is not overfitting.

For our last models below we can see the scatter plot shows that the MLP model captures the overall positive relationship between NBA player stats and salary. However, predictions for high-salary players tend to be underestimated, suggesting the model struggles with the nonlinearity or outliers in very high compensation. The MAE shows that on average, the model’s predictions are off by about $5.73 million. Lastly, the error chart shows that this model tends to underpredict, and occasionally over predict salaries for some of the players.
